title: Querying and scanning: CollectRows, RowToStructByName, NULL handling
summary: pgx.CollectRows with RowToStructByName turns rows into typed structs and does the close-and-check bookkeeping for you. Give every nullable column a type that can say NULL (*string, pgtype.Text), because pgx refuses to scan NULL into a zero value.

examples.title: CollectRows, RowTo and CollectOneRow, and how strict name mapping is

annotations.note: Fields match columns by name, ignoring case and, for untagged fields, underscores (pgx 5.5.2+), so BirthYear finds birth_year. A db:"col" tag pins the name, db:"-" skips the field, unexported fields are ignored.

Exec with no arguments uses PostgreSQL's simple protocol, which takes several statements in one string: handy for setup. With arguments, pgx sends one statement and the values separately, which is what makes parameters injection-proof (next lesson).

CollectRows loops, scans, closes the rows and checks rows.Err(): the four steps a hand-written loop gets wrong. Ignoring Query's error is the documented style here, because CollectRows returns the same error.
RowTo[T] covers single-column results. CollectRows always returns a non-nil slice, so zero rows encode to JSON as [] rather than null.

No row is an error, not a zero User. pgx.ErrNoRows wraps sql.ErrNoRows (pgx 5.7+), so either check works. Translate it to your own ErrNotFound at the repository boundary, as the errors module did with *pgconn.PgError.

Name mapping is strict: a column without a field fails, and so does a field without a column. With SELECT *, an ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN breaks binaries already deployed. RowToStructByNameLax only forgives missing columns, not extra ones; list the columns.

examples.title: NULL in, NULL out, and the aggregate that returns NULL

annotations.note: Nullability goes into the type. *string reads naturally and encodes to JSON null; pgtype.Text is what sqlc generates for pgx. sql.NullString and sql.Null[string] (Go 1.22) work too, because pgx accepts any sql.Scanner.
A nil pointer, an untyped nil or pgtype.Text{} is sent as NULL. The empty string is a value: Gül is known to have no phone, Ömer's is unknown, and the database keeps the difference.
NULL into a plain string is an error that names the column. pgx won't invent "" for you; JDBC's getString would have handed you null, and getInt a silent 0.
The two rows keep "" and NULL apart. A NULL pgtype.Text still has String == "", so check Valid first; with *string, forgetting the nil check panics on dereference instead of printing a fake value.
Except for count, aggregates over zero rows return NULL: sum of nothing is NULL, not 0. Here coalesce is honest, because no orders really means a quantity of 0.

use_cases: CollectRows + RowToStructByName: list endpoints, reports, anything that maps rows onto a struct
RowTo[T]: single-column results such as ids or names
QueryRow / CollectOneRow: lookups by key, where no row becomes a domain-level not found
ForEachRow: large results processed row by row without building a slice
strengths: Unlike a JDBC ResultSet loop, CollectRows closes the rows and checks the error in one call, so the two classic mistakes can't happen
Mapping mistakes are loud: an extra or missing column is an error, unlike encoding/json, which silently leaves unknown fields at their zero value
NULL cannot become a zero value by accident: scanning it into string or int64 fails and names the column
Generics give typed results ([]User) without an ORM or code generation
weaknesses: Names are matched at run time: a typo in a db tag or a column alias is a runtime error, which sqlc (lesson 5) moves to generation time
RowToStructByName matches columns by reflection (cached per struct and column list); a hand-written Scan, which sqlc generates, skips even that
Three spellings of a nullable value (*T, pgtype.T, sql.Null[T]) invite a codebase that mixes all of them

pitfalls.title: SELECT * into a struct
pitfalls.detail: Adding a column to the table breaks every RowToStructByName over SELECT * until the struct catches up. List the columns you map.
pitfalls.bad:
rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT * FROM users")
users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
pitfalls.good:
rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users")
users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])

pitfalls.title: coalesce to make NULL go away
pitfalls.detail: coalesce(phone, '') merges "unknown" with "known to be empty". Use it where NULL really means zero (an aggregate over no rows); elsewhere scan into a nullable type.

pitfalls.title: Reading pgtype.Text.String without Valid
pitfalls.detail: A NULL pgtype.Text has String == "". Check Valid first, or use *string so a NULL can't pass for a value.

pitfalls.title: A hand-written loop without rows.Err()
pitfalls.detail: Next returns false at the end and on a network error alike. Without the Err check, a failure halfway through looks like a short result.

pitfalls.title: Building an IN list by hand
pitfalls.detail: Pass a Go slice as one parameter and compare with = any($1). IN ($1) compares against the whole array, and string-joining ids into the SQL is the injection the next lesson is about.
pitfalls.bad: q := "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id IN (" + strings.Join(ids, ",") + ")"
pitfalls.good: rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = any($1)", ids)

quiz.q: A query uses SELECT * with RowToStructByName[User]. A colleague adds a nullable column to the table. What happens to the binary already deployed?
options: Scanning fails: the struct has no field for the new column
The column lands in the nearest matching field
quiz.why: Every column must have a field (and every field a column); extra columns are an error even with the Lax variant.

quiz.q: Which Go type honestly represents a nullable text column?
quiz.why: Both can say NULL. Scanning NULL into string is an error in pgx, and "" would conflate unknown with empty anyway.

quiz.q: SELECT max(created_at) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1, for a customer with no orders, scanned into a time.Time. What happens?
options: An error: cannot scan NULL into *time.Time
quiz.why: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; over zero input rows its value is NULL. Scan into *time.Time or use coalesce.

quiz.q: CollectOneRow found no rows. Which checks are true?
options: Both errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) and errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)
err is nil and the value is the zero struct
quiz.why: Since pgx 5.7, pgx.ErrNoRows unwraps to sql.ErrNoRows.

body:
## Concept

`Query` returns `pgx.Rows`, a cursor over the result that holds a connection until it is
closed. Don't loop over it by hand; hand it to a collector together with a function that
turns one row into a value:

- `pgx.CollectRows(rows, fn)` returns `[]T`; `CollectOneRow` returns the first `T` or
  `pgx.ErrNoRows`; `CollectExactlyOneRow` also fails with `ErrTooManyRows`.
- `fn` is usually `pgx.RowTo[T]` (one column), `pgx.RowToStructByName[T]` (columns to
  fields by name) or `RowToStructByPos[T]` (by position). The `RowToAddrOf...` variants
  return `*T`.
- `ForEachRow` scans into variables you provide and calls a function per row: no slice.

All of them close the rows and check `rows.Err()`. `QueryRow(...).Scan(...)` remains the
shortest way to read one row into variables.

Go has no null string or null int, so a nullable column needs a type that can hold
NULL: a pointer (`*string`, nil for NULL), a `pgtype` value (`pgtype.Text`, with `Valid`),
or `sql.Null[T]`. Scanning NULL into a plain `string` or `int64` is an error, which is the
point: the struct you scan into should say what the schema says.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: JDBC's `getInt` returns 0 for NULL unless you remember `wasNull()`; Go makes you
  pick a NULL-capable type up front, and fails loudly if you didn't. `CollectRows` with
  `RowToStructByName` is roughly Spring's `BeanPropertyRowMapper` without the framework.
- Python: psycopg hands back `None` for NULL in any column. Go strings can't be `nil`, so
  `*string` or `pgtype.Text` plays `None`'s role.
- JS/TS: node-postgres puts `null` in the row object and TypeScript believes whatever type
  you declared. pgx checks every value as it scans.
- C: libpq's `PQgetisnull` is the `Valid` flag of `pgtype.Text`, minus the struct.

## Design notes

Treat the struct as the contract with the schema: `NOT NULL` columns get plain types,
nullable ones get `*T` (or `pgtype.T` if you follow sqlc's output), and the query lists its
columns. Pick one nullable spelling per codebase; pointers are plain Go and encode to JSON
`null`, as does `pgtype.Text`.

`coalesce` is for places where NULL really means zero, such as the sum of no rows.
Turning an unknown phone number into `""` loses information you can't get back.

Keep `pgx.ErrNoRows` inside the repository: return your own `ErrNotFound` (wrapped with
`%w`) so callers never import pgx, which is the translation rule from the errors module.

Text comparison is exact: `WHERE city = $1` matches `İzmir` byte for byte. For
case-insensitive Turkish matching, remember this database's builtin `C.UTF-8` locale
lowercases `I` to `i`, never `ı`; Turkish rules need an explicit ICU collation such as
`lower(city COLLATE "tr-x-icu")`, which the `sql.search` module covers.

package main

import (
	"context"
	"database/sql"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
)

type User struct {
	ID        int64
	Name      string
	City      string
	BirthYear int32 // matches birth_year: case and underscores are ignored
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	conn, err := pgx.Connect(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer conn.Close(ctx)

	_, err = conn.Exec(ctx, `
		CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
			name text NOT NULL, city text NOT NULL, birth_year int NOT NULL);
		INSERT INTO users (name, city, birth_year)
		VALUES ('Ayşe', 'İzmir', 1990), ('Çağrı', 'Ankara', 1985), ('Işıl', 'İzmir', 2001)`)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	const byCity = "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users WHERE city = $1 ORDER BY id"
	rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx, byCity, "İzmir") // errors resurface from CollectRows
	users, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Printf("%+v %v\n", users, err)

	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT name FROM users ORDER BY id")
	names, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowTo[string])
	fmt.Println(names, err)

	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name, city, birth_year FROM users WHERE id = $1", 99)
	_, err = pgx.CollectOneRow(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Println(err, errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows), errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows))

	// Someone adds a column; SELECT * now returns a field User doesn't have.
	if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx, "ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone text"); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	rows, _ = conn.Query(ctx, "SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id")
	_, err = pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[User])
	fmt.Println(err)
}
